title: A (very) short read about memory and learning...
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton uses Lisa Genova's book Remember as a stress test of the core ideas behind his Looking for Learning series, and finds they hold. He revisits four agreements: learning happens in the brain, it depends on appropriate repeated experiences, knowledge, skills and understanding are learned and assessed differently, and memory is an outcome of learning rather than a separate factor. Genova's account of the hippocampus handling knowledge while the basal ganglia and cerebellum handle skills is offered as neuroscientific support for treating the two differently. The most interesting move is his explanation of why memory never made his list of twelve factors affecting learning: it is the sticky residue of repeated experience, so a bad memory really reflects weak attention and too little repetition. The post ends as a reassurance that the framework is still sound as a new season begins.
points: Learning is located in the brain, not in classrooms or muscles, so teaching has to work with how brains actually build and keep things.
Repeated experience is the engine of learning, and an overfull curriculum quietly trades repetition for mere coverage.
Genova's distinction between the hippocampal route for knowledge and the basal ganglia and cerebellar route for skills backs the claim that the two need different teaching and assessment.
Memory is a product of learning, not a cause, so a poor memory points to attention and repetition problems rather than a fixed deficit.
quotes: Our answer is that learning takes place in the brain. Learning is a brain thing.

I have written and said everywhere that the core experience of learning is repeated experiences, and that without those repeated experiences learning is unlikely to happen. A consequence of this is that an over-full curriculum, too little time in lessons (and other things, too) all contribute to repeated experiences losing out to simple coverage.

Genova shows how knowledge learning (I know that Paris is the capital of France) is processed through short-term working memory into long-term memory through the hippocampus. Skills learning (I am able to navigate my way to Paris), on the other hand, occurs through a part of the brain called the basal ganglia and then reinforced through the cerebellum. She says that ‘while the hippocampus is essential for forming…knowledge…this brain structure isn’t involved at all in creating’ skills.

I spent way too long trying to work out how to use memory as one of the core factors that affect learning. Now I know why I failed and why I am glad I didn’t try to squeeze it in somewhere. It’s because memory is the result of learning and not independent of it.
Memory is what happens when learning is made sticky through repeated experiences. Memory is the result of the learning experience and not a factor that contributes to it.

Having a ‘bad’ memory is caused by not paying initial attention, not being given the right learning experiences and not having the repeated experiences to make the learning sticky. There is no memory that is bad of its own accord.
